children: India’s engineering talent pipeline is seeing a shift in skills and employment outcomes, as companies seek engineers who combine technical foundations with practical exposure and newer technologies

India has a large pool of engineering graduates, but ensuring that enough of them move into core engineering roles is critical to supporting the country’s industrial expansion. As manufacturing adopts more automation and digital technologies, companies are looking for engineers who bring strong grounding in traditional disciplines alongside the ability to work with newer technologies.

According to the latest available AICTE data for 2024-25, the placement rate for Computer Science and Engineering (CSE) students stood at 94.46 per cent, compared with 66.48 per cent for mechanical engineering, 58.58 per cent for electrical engineering and 41.88 per cent for civil engineering. The difference in placement outcomes points to the stronger employment pull of technology-oriented branches, even as industries continue to require engineers from traditional disciplines.

For core engineering, the issue is therefore not simply the number of graduates being produced, but how well those graduates are prepared for industrial roles. Engineering education needs to translate into the ability to work with physical systems, equipment, production processes and testing, while also preparing engineers to work with the digital technologies now being integrated into these environments.

According to Niti Aayog’s 2026 report on education and skilling, employability among BE/BTech graduates stood at 70.2 per cent in 2026, down from 71.5 per cent in 2025. While the figure has risen from 57.1 per cent in 2019, Niti Aayog said the relatively slow improvement in BE/BTech employability points to the need for better pedagogy, updated laboratory equipment and stronger industry linkages.

That gap is relevant as core engineering roles evolve beyond conventional technical functions. Engineers are expected to combine their disciplinary knowledge with practical problem-solving and an ability to work with automation, software and artificial intelligence as these technologies become embedded in industrial environments.
The Core Engineer Is Changing

L&T Technology Services (LTTS) said India’s manufacturing ambitions will depend not only on attracting more engineers into core sectors, but also on “reimagining what a core engineer looks like in the age of AI”. As products, factories and infrastructure become more software-defined and intelligent, engineers will need a combination of domain expertise, strong foundational knowledge and AI fluency.

“We see AI as an enabler that elevates engineering expertise rather than replaces it. Our Engineering Intelligence approach enables engineers to focus on innovation, architecture, validation, and complex problem-solving. For Make in India to achieve its full potential, India needs engineers who can not only build products, but also orchestrate AI, apply judgment, and translate innovation into globally competitive real-world outcomes,” LTTS said.

The company said its efforts to develop this talent include its annual Techgium event, collaborations with academic institutions and programmes focused on emerging engineering capabilities. In FY26, LTTS completed 5,78,212 hours of learning, averaging 4.57 training days per employee, as it builds AI-enabled capabilities across software, embedded systems and domain engineering.
The shift does not make traditional engineering disciplines less relevant. Instead, strong engineering fundamentals are becoming the base for newer digital, automation and AI capabilities.
Fundamentals Still Matter

Sriram Lakshminarayanan, President, Honeywell Technology & Connected Solutions (HTCS), Honeywell Technologies, said disciplines such as mechanical, electrical, industrial and automation engineering will play a central role in building the products and industrial capabilities that define the next phase of Make in India.

According to Lakshminarayanan, many of the technologies powering industrial automation, critical infrastructure, smart buildings and energy transition are already being engineered in India for global markets. “As manufacturing becomes more digital and connected, core engineering talent will be essential to accelerating India's industrial growth and global competitiveness,” he said.

This makes the quality of engineering preparation as important as the number of graduates entering the workforce. Strong fundamentals need to be complemented by practical exposure and the ability to apply engineering knowledge to complex systems.
From Prototypes To Production
The shift is also evident in specialised engineering roles, where engineers are expected to take technical concepts through development and into products that can perform reliably at scale.

Ponni Carlin, Co-Founder & COO, iVP Semi, said engineering capabilities across design, testing, packaging and manufacturing are supporting India’s semiconductor ambitions. As the country builds greater self-reliance in semiconductors, engineers are taking on a broader role that extends beyond developing prototypes to ensuring products can meet real-world performance and manufacturing requirements.

“Greater emphasis is now being placed on engineering judgement, product qualification, energy efficiency, manufacturability, and system performance, alongside innovation in chip design. With automation and AI taking on repetitive tasks, greater value is being created through the ability to solve complex problems and translate engineering innovation into products that can perform reliably at scale,” Carlin said.

The example reflects a wider shift in core engineering. The engineer is no longer defined only by a degree or a particular discipline, but by the ability to apply that technical foundation across design, production, validation and intelligent industrial systems.
Connecting Education And Industry

For India, this makes the connection between engineering education and industry central to the talent challenge. The stronger employment outcomes in technology-oriented branches show why students may gravitate to them. Niti Aayog’s assessment highlights the need to strengthen the employability of engineering graduates more broadly.

The task is not simply to produce more engineering graduates or push students towards particular branches. It is to ensure those entering core roles have the technical grounding, practical experience and adaptability required to work across modern industrial systems.

For Make in India, the challenge is to convert India’s large engineering graduate pool into a stronger pipeline of talent for core roles. The core engineer of the future will still need to understand physical systems and engineering principles, but will also need to work confidently with automation, digital technologies and AI.
